Making Japanese curry? 🍛  Don’t just chop everything into random sizes. The way you cut your vegetables actually matters, especially if you want them nicely cooked and not disappear in curry. 🥕 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐨𝐭 → rangiri cut Cutting it into irregular rolling pieces gives you different surfaces while keeping the pieces relatively similar in size, so they cook evenly. 🥔 𝐏𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐨 → bite-size chunks Not too small, so they have enough structure to hold their shape while becoming tender. 🧅 𝐎𝐧𝐢𝐨𝐧 → wedges Keeping the onion in wedges allows it to soften and become sweet without completely disappearing into the curry. It’s a small step, but proper cutting makes a difference in cooking time, texture and how your curry comes together. Let’s make Ragi mudde  A popular dish from Karnataka that replaces rice in a South Indian meal. Although an acquired taste, this humble dish packs in a ton of nutrition and is great to sop up any curry. In 2 cups of water, mix 1/2 cup ragi flour. Mix and boil until it is a little thick. This thick porridge-y concoction is Ragi Ambali, another spectacular dish. Take out 1/2 the ambali in a cup. Now to the remaining ambali in the pot, add in 1.5 cups of Ragi flour, mix coarsely, close the lid and set on the lowest heat/flame. After 10 mins, open the lid, turn off the heat and mix away until well combined.  I couldn’t show this part in the photos because one hand and not a professional tiktoker 🤷‍♀️ In a separate bowl laced with ghee and keeping a small bowl of water on the side, you add a nice chunk of the ragi mudde into the ghee bowl, wet your hands with the water nearby, and take the mudde to make a ball using the ghee bowl. A little knead and ball action gets it smooth and round into the perfect little mudde. Store in an air tight container until ready to consume. #ragi #ragimudde #food #india #indianfood
